title: Conditional GAN-based synthetic financial modeling for street vendors in India's informal economy
summary: Surveys 1000 street vendors across three cities in Odisha and trains a small fairness-aware conditional GAN on nine socio-demographic and behavioural attributes, on the argument that informal-sector records are too few and too irregular for the credit-risk and fraud models that formal finance runs on. The generator is a three-layer MLP with fairness-aware loss reweighting rather than any existing tabular architecture, and the paper reports Frechet distance 10.12, behavioural entropy 3.59 bits, gains of 3.2 and 2.9 percent on loan-default prediction and anomaly detection from hybrid real-plus-synthetic training, and demographic-parity deviation held under 2.4 percent by audits every 50 epochs. CTGAN is the closest prior adversarial baseline and is trained and sampled on the same preprocessed dataset with aligned normalization and conditional inputs, losing to the proposed model on every reported measure. It appears only in that comparison role, so the entry records CTGAN as the benchmark a new generator is measured against.
evidence: section 2.2 states that CTGAN (Xu et al., 2019) introduces mode-specific normalization for mixed-type tabular data and supports limited categorical conditioning; section 2.3 states that CTGAN introduces mode-specific normalization and Gumbel-softmax encoding to handle mixed-type tabular data but that its training stability degrades in low-resource regimes, often requiring more than 10,000 samples to converge meaningfully; section 3.5 lists CTGAN as one of three benchmarked generative models, described as a conditional tabular GAN designed for mixed-type tabular data serving as the closest prior adversarial baseline, with all baselines implemented on the same preprocessed dataset of 1000 vendor profiles; table 3 reports CTGAN (baseline) at FD 12.42, MMD 0.023, entropy 3.47 and loan accuracy 76.1 percent against the proposed cGAN at 10.12, 0.019, 3.59 and 81.6 percent; table 1 lists CTGAN under general tabular data with partial categorical conditional inputs. NOTE: the bibliography also carries a reference to Xu and Veeramachaneni (2019), 'Creditgan: Generating fair synthetic credit data', arXiv:1801.02396, which does not correspond to any known work by those authors and is cited in the text as a distinct model from CTGAN

title: An approach for cancer outcomes modelling using a comprehensive synthetic dataset
venue: Physical and Engineering Sciences in Medicine
summary: Observes that work on synthetic medical data has concentrated on generating images, from which radiomic features must then be extracted and which carry no prognostic information, and proposes instead to synthesize the radiomic features and the clinical record together so that a virtual patient is a single coherent row. Working from 132 non-small cell lung cancer patients in the public Lung1 cohort, the authors generate 106 virtual patients and train two-year overall survival models across four feature-selection methods and six classifiers, on real or synthetic data separately, testing on withheld real data and externally validating on a second cohort; XGBoost with random-forest importance features differs by under 1.3 percent between the two training sources. CTGAN is the only generator: version 0.13.0 is trained for 300 epochs with the Adam optimizer, its embedding and generator dimensions and learning rates are swept, constraints are specified to keep radiomic features standardized, ages non-negative and clinical features one-hot encoded, and fidelity is read off CTGAN's own built-in metric, one minus the Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic. The entire study therefore rests on running the SDV generator, down to its constraint interface and its packaged evaluation metric.

evidence: the introduction states that conditional tabular generative adversarial networks (CTGANs), reference 17, have been developed to simultaneously generate mixed datasets, reference 17 being Xu, Skoularidou, Cuesta-Infante and Veeramachaneni, Modeling tabular data using conditional GAN, NeurIPS 2019; the model development pipeline states that a Conditional Tabular Generative Adversarial Network (CTGAN) reference 17 version 0.13.0 model was trained to generate a synthetic training dataset of radiomic and clinical features, trained for 300 epochs using the Adam optimizer, and that constraints were specified to generate standardized radiomic features, non-negative age values (positive constraint), and one-hot encoded clinical features; the same passage states that performance was evaluated using CTGAN's built-in metric based on a two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, 1 minus the KS statistic D; table 2 sweeps the CTGAN hyperparameters embedding_dim, generator_dim, generator_lr and discriminator_lr; the discussion states that the CTGAN model was designed to generate synthetic data within the distribution of real data and that generating 106 synthetic patients took 90.1 ms, 2667 times faster than a comparable synthetic-image workflow; the bibliography also carries DP-CTGAN (reference 47)

title: Generative models for tabular data: A review
venue: Journal of Mechanical Science and Technology
summary: Reviews tabular generative modelling for readers coming from engineering design, first laying out notation for mixed continuous and discrete attributes and the model families available, from decision trees and random forests through MLPs, VAEs and GANs to Gaussian processes and Bayesian networks, then organizing the literature by what the generated data is for: differential privacy, missing-value interpolation, data distribution modelling, and data augmentation. Each objective gets a table of reported results by dataset and metric, and the paper closes on four standing difficulties, namely non-normal distributions, imbalanced categories, unstable adversarial training and outliers. CTGAN is placed as the pivot of the distribution-modelling literature: the review credits Xu et al. with preprocessing that handles multi-modal continuous attributes by Gaussian mixture normalization and imbalanced discrete attributes by training-by-sampling, and states that these methods went on to influence several subsequent studies. Nothing is implemented or run anywhere in the review, so the entry records a survey that treats CTGAN as the reference point of its field.
evidence: section 3.3 states that in 2019 Xu et al., reference 8, proposed a conditional GAN model that not only addressed non-ideal distributions of tabular data but also tackled class imbalance issues, that continuous attributes were normalized for multi-modal distributions using GMM while discrete attributes were addressed using the training-by-sampling method, and that the data preprocessing methods demonstrated by Xu et al., reference 14, have influenced several subsequent studies on generating tabular data; section 3.4 names CTGAN, reference 14, alongside beta-VAE as the high-performance deep learning models whose deep and complex network structures require significant training data; section 4.1 states that efforts by Xu et al., reference 14, and Tai et al. address abnormal distributions using Gaussian mixture models as a preprocessing step; the bibliography carries both Xu et al. 2019, Modeling tabular data using conditional GAN (reference 14), and Xu and Veeramachaneni 2018, Synthesizing tabular data using generative adversarial networks, arXiv:1811.11264 (reference 42); table 3 reports CTGAN results by dataset drawn from the cited papers rather than from any run by the reviewers
